questions.stem: The Parliament of Queensland is described as unicameral because it:
options: consists of the Crown, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council
can make laws only on matters listed in section 51 of the Constitution
shares its law-making power equally with local government councils
consists of the Crown and a single house, the Legislative Assembly
questions.explanation: Queensland's Constitution Act 1867 provides that the Parliament consists of the Sovereign and the Legislative Assembly, with no upper house. Queensland is the only Australian state with one house; the Legislative Council was abolished in 1922.

questions.stem: In which year was Queensland's upper house, the Legislative Council, abolished?
questions.explanation: The Constitution Act Amendment Act 1922 (Qld) abolished the Legislative Council, leaving the Legislative Assembly as the only house. 1901 is the year of Federation, when the Commonwealth Parliament first met.

questions.stem: A Queensland government wants to create a new upper house to review bills. Under the Constitution Act Amendment Act 1934 (Qld), what must happen before the bill can receive assent?
options: It must be referred to the High Court for an advisory opinion
It must be approved by Queensland electors at a referendum
It must be approved by a double majority in a national referendum
It must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the Commonwealth Parliament
questions.explanation: Section 3 of the 1934 Act says the Parliament cannot be altered to re-establish a Legislative Council or another legislative body unless the bill is first approved by Queensland electors at a referendum. A national double majority applies only to changes to the Australian Constitution under section 128.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant implication of Queensland having a unicameral parliament?
options: Laws made by Queensland can never be inconsistent with valid Commonwealth laws
No upper house reviews bills, so a majority government faces fewer checks
Bills must pass two houses, so a government without a Senate majority cannot make laws
The Governor can amend bills passed by the Legislative Assembly before giving assent
questions.explanation: Without a house of review, a government holding a majority in the Legislative Assembly can usually pass its bills without amendment by another chamber. This is why committees and other accountability bodies matter more in Queensland. The Senate is part of the Commonwealth Parliament, not the Queensland Parliament.

questions.stem: Because Queensland has no upper house, its parliamentary rules require that each bill be:
options: examined by a portfolio committee, normally for at least six weeks
approved by a majority of local government mayors before it is introduced
checked by the High Court for validity before the Governor gives assent
passed twice by the Legislative Assembly, with a general election in between
questions.explanation: The Legislative Assembly's Standing Orders, made under the Parliament of Queensland Act 2001, refer each bill to a portfolio committee, normally for at least six weeks, which lets the public make submissions and gives some of the scrutiny an upper house would provide. The High Court decides validity only when a case comes before it.

questions.stem: The Queensland Government declares a bill urgent and passes it within two days without committee examination. Which statement best evaluates this?
options: It is invalid, because every bill must spend six weeks before a committee without exception
It is lawful, because committees in Queensland have no role in examining bills
It is invalid, because only the Governor can declare a bill to be urgent
It is lawful, but it removes the committee scrutiny that partly replaces an upper house
questions.explanation: The Standing Orders allow the Legislative Assembly, by ordinary majority, to declare a bill urgent and shorten or skip committee referral. This is lawful, but in a unicameral parliament it removes the main formal check on a bill, so it is often criticised as weakening accountability.

questions.stem: Before a Queensland bill becomes law, after passing the Legislative Assembly it must:
options: be passed by the Senate on behalf of the states
receive royal assent from the Governor
receive royal assent from the Governor-General
be approved by the Queensland Court of Appeal
questions.explanation: Every bill passed by the Legislative Assembly is presented to the Governor of Queensland, the King's representative in the state, for assent. The Governor-General gives assent to Commonwealth bills, not state bills.

questions.stem: A member of the Legislative Assembly introduces a bill. Under the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld), the member must table:
options: a statement of compatibility with human rights
a certificate from the Governor confirming the bill is within state power
a report from the Queensland Law Reform Commission recommending the bill
a petition showing that a majority of electors support the bill
questions.explanation: Section 38 requires a member introducing a bill to prepare a statement of compatibility stating whether, in the member's opinion, it is compatible with human rights and, if not, the nature and extent of the incompatibility. It applies to government and private members' bills.

questions.stem: Since a 2016 referendum, when are ordinary general elections for the Queensland Parliament held?
options: On the last Saturday in October, every four years
On a date chosen by the Premier, at least every three years
On the same day as each federal election for the Senate
On the first Saturday in March, every five years
questions.explanation: Queensland voters approved fixed four-year terms at a referendum in 2016. The Constitution of Queensland now sets the normal polling day as the last Saturday in October in the fourth calendar year after the previous ordinary election.

questions.stem: Which level of government is created by state legislation rather than by the Australian Constitution?
options: The Commonwealth government, based in Canberra
The state government, based in Brisbane
The territory government of the Northern Territory
Local government, such as Brisbane City Council
questions.explanation: Local councils in Queensland are established and given their powers by state law, mainly the Local Government Act 2009 (Qld). The Commonwealth and the original states are recognised by the Australian Constitution; territories are created by Commonwealth law.

questions.stem: A Queensland council makes a local law requiring dogs to be kept on a leash in parks. Which statement about this law is correct?
options: It is valid only if made within the powers that state legislation gives the council
It is valid only if approved by the Commonwealth Parliament under section 51
It overrides any inconsistent Queensland Act, because it was made more recently
It must be approved by a referendum of the council's residents to take effect
questions.explanation: Councils have only the law-making powers given to them by state legislation, so a local law beyond those powers, or inconsistent with a state Act, is invalid. A later local law does not override a state Act.

questions.stem: In the Northern Territory, the role of the Crown in giving assent to laws passed by the Legislative Assembly is performed by the:
options: Chief Minister
Governor of Queensland
Administrator
Governor-General
questions.explanation: Territory Administrators represent the Crown in some territories, including the Northern Territory. The Chief Minister heads the territory government but does not represent the Crown, and the Governor-General acts for the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of the Governor of Queensland?
options: The presiding officer of the Legislative Assembly, who keeps order during debates
The chief judge of Queensland, who decides whether state laws are constitutionally valid
The King's representative, who gives assent and acts on ministers' advice
The head of the Queensland Government, who chooses ministers and leads the majority party
questions.explanation: The Governor represents the Crown in Queensland, gives royal assent to bills and appoints ministers, acting by convention on the advice of the Premier and ministers. The Premier leads the government, the Speaker presides over the Assembly, and the Chief Justice heads the Supreme Court.

questions.stem: Responsible government in Queensland means that:
options: the Governor is personally responsible to voters for every decision of the government
judges are elected by the people and can be removed at the next general election
the government is responsible to the Commonwealth Parliament for its state laws
the Premier and ministers sit in parliament and need the Assembly's confidence
questions.explanation: Ministers are drawn from parliament and are collectively and individually answerable to it, so a government that loses the confidence of the Assembly must resign or seek an election. Judges in Australia are appointed, not elected.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth wants to improve state school literacy, even though education is a residual power. Which mechanism is it most likely to use?
options: Grants to the states under section 96 with conditions on how money is spent
A law under section 109 declaring education an exclusive Commonwealth power
A referendum under section 128 held only in the states that oppose the plan
An order of the High Court directing the states to adopt a national curriculum
questions.explanation: Section 96 lets the Commonwealth give financial assistance to a state on terms and conditions it sets, so tied grants allow it to influence residual areas such as schools and hospitals. Section 109 only resolves inconsistency between valid laws; it does not create new powers.

questions.stem: A party wins 50 of the 93 seats in the Queensland Legislative Assembly. What is the most likely effect on law-making?
options: The government must negotiate with the Senate before any state bill can pass
The government needs crossbench support to pass every bill it introduces
The government cannot pass bills until the Governor approves its policies
The government can usually pass its bills, as no upper house can block them
questions.explanation: A party with a majority in Queensland's single house controls the only chamber that votes on bills, so it can usually pass its legislation. Crossbench support is needed only by a minority government, and the Senate plays no part in state law-making.

questions.stem: A minority government is one that:
options: is formed when a referendum to change the Constitution is not carried
lacks a majority in the lower house and relies on crossbench members to govern
won fewer than half of the seats in the Senate at the last federal election
represents a party that received less than half of the national primary vote
questions.explanation: A minority government does not hold a majority of seats in the house where government is formed, so it relies on independents or minor parties for confidence, supply and the passage of bills. Lacking a Senate majority does not make a government a minority government.

questions.stem: In 2005 the federal government gained a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, and soon passed the WorkChoices industrial relations laws. Which statement best evaluates this kind of majority?
options: It means the High Court cannot review the laws, because both houses have approved them
It requires every bill to be approved at a referendum, so it slows down reform
It gives the states a veto over the laws, because the Senate is the states' house
It allows quick reform, but it weakens the Senate as a house of review
questions.explanation: When a government controls both houses, the Senate is less likely to amend or reject its bills, so reform can be fast but receives less scrutiny. The High Court can still decide whether such laws are valid, as it did in the WorkChoices case.

questions.stem: Under section 57 of the Constitution, a double dissolution may occur when:
options: the Queensland Legislative Assembly and the Governor disagree over a bill
a referendum fails to win a majority of voters in a majority of the states
the High Court declares that a Commonwealth Act is beyond federal power
the Senate twice rejects a bill from the lower house, three months apart
questions.explanation: If the Senate twice rejects or fails to pass a bill, with an interval of three months, the Governor-General may dissolve both houses at once. A double dissolution applies only to the Commonwealth Parliament, which has two houses.

questions.stem: After a double dissolution election, the Senate again rejects the bill that triggered it. What can happen next under section 57?
options: A joint sitting of both houses may vote on it, and it passes with an absolute majority of all members
The Governor-General may give assent without any further vote, because the election decided the issue
The bill is put to a national referendum and needs a double majority to pass
The House of Representatives may pass it alone if two-thirds of its members agree
questions.explanation: The Governor-General may convene a joint sitting, where the bill passes if an absolute majority of the total members of both houses votes for it. The only joint sitting so far was held in 1974. A referendum is needed only to change the Constitution.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares law-making in the Queensland and Commonwealth parliaments?
options: Queensland bills need a double dissolution to pass, whereas Commonwealth bills need only one house
Both parliaments need a referendum to pass any bill opposed by the upper house
Both parliaments require the High Court to approve bills before royal assent
Commonwealth bills can be blocked by an upper house, whereas Queensland bills face no second chamber
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Parliament is bicameral, so the Senate can amend or reject bills, and section 57 sets out how deadlocks are resolved. Queensland is unicameral, so double dissolutions and joint sittings do not arise there.

questions.stem: Which Queensland court hears criminal charges against young people under the Youth Justice Act 1992 (Qld)?
options: The Childrens Court of Queensland
The Land Court of Queensland
The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal
questions.explanation: The Childrens Court deals with charges against children under the Youth Justice Act, and also with child protection matters. It is constituted by a Childrens Court judge for serious matters and by a magistrate for others. The Family Court hears family law disputes, not criminal charges.

questions.stem: Unlike most courts, the Childrens Court of Queensland must generally exclude members of the public. Which is the main reason for this?
options: To keep the outcome secret from the child's victims
To protect the child's privacy and support rehabilitation
To allow the child to give evidence without taking an oath
To let the magistrate decide the case without any lawyers
questions.explanation: Hearings involving children are closed to the general public to protect the young person's identity and give them a better chance of rehabilitation. The Act still allows people such as the child's family, victims and accredited media to be present.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Murri Court in Queensland?
options: A sentencing process in which Elders and Respected Persons give the magistrate cultural advice
A separate court in which Elders decide guilt and sentence under customary law
A tribunal that hears native title claims over pastoral leases in Queensland
A federal court that reviews visa decisions affecting First Nations people
questions.explanation: The Murri Court operates within the Magistrates and Childrens Courts for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander defendants who plead guilty. Elders and Respected Persons provide cultural advice, but the magistrate still sentences under Queensland law. It does not apply customary law or decide guilt.

questions.stem: The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) can review:
options: appeals from criminal convictions entered by juries in the District Court
decisions of the High Court on the meaning of the Australian Constitution
many decisions made by Queensland government agencies, as well as resolving civil disputes
decisions of Commonwealth agencies such as Services Australia and the Home Affairs department
questions.explanation: QCAT resolves disputes such as tenancy and minor civil claims and reviews many administrative decisions made by Queensland government bodies. Decisions of Commonwealth agencies are reviewed by the Administrative Review Tribunal.

questions.stem: A Centrelink decision cancels a person's payment. Which body could review the decision on its merits?
options: The Queensland Court of Appeal
The Administrative Review Tribunal
The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal
The Childrens Court of Queensland
questions.explanation: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART), which replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in 2024, reviews Commonwealth government decisions, such as social security, visa and NDIS decisions, on their merits. QCAT reviews Queensland government decisions.

questions.stem: Which court deals with divorce and parenting disputes under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)?
options: The Magistrates Court of Queensland
The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
The Childrens Court of Queensland
The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal
questions.explanation: Family law is a Commonwealth matter, so it is heard in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, formed in 2021 by bringing together the Family Court and the Federal Circuit Court. The Childrens Court deals with youth justice and child protection, which are state matters.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates specialist courts and tribunals in achieving just and equitable outcomes?
options: Their expertise and informality can improve access, but limited resources can cause delays
They guarantee identical outcomes in every case, so they remove the need for appeals
They apply less law than other courts, so their decisions cannot be reviewed
They replace parliament as law-makers, so they make laws faster than parliament
questions.explanation: Specialist bodies can be cheaper, quicker and less formal and have judges or members with expertise in the area, which can improve access to justice. However, heavy workloads and limited funding can lead to delays, and their decisions can still be appealed or reviewed.

questions.stem: In Wik Peoples v Queensland (1996), the High Court held that:
options: the Commonwealth could not make laws about native title because it is a residual power
pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title over the land
native title could never exist over land in Queensland that had been granted to anyone else
terra nullius was a valid basis for British sovereignty over the whole of Australia
questions.explanation: The Court held by majority that native title could coexist with pastoral leases, with the pastoralist's rights prevailing where they conflicted. Parliament responded with the Native Title Amendment Act 1998 (Cth), showing how a court decision can prompt legislative change.

questions.stem: In New South Wales v Commonwealth (2006), the WorkChoices case, the High Court upheld national workplace laws under the:
options: corporations power in section 51(xx)
external affairs power in section 51(xxix)
defence power in section 51(vi)
trade and commerce power in section 51(i)
questions.explanation: The majority held the Commonwealth could regulate the workplace relations of constitutional corporations under section 51(xx). The decision greatly widened the corporations power and moved much of industrial relations away from the states. The external affairs power was the basis of the Tasmanian Dam case.

questions.stem: In Roadshow Films v iiNet (2012), the High Court held that an internet provider had not authorised its customers' illegal downloading of films. Which later change best shows the relationship between case law and legislation?
options: The High Court overruled its own decision two years later after a new case on the same facts
The Federal Court distinguished the decision and ordered iiNet to pay damages to film studios
The states passed laws under section 109 making internet providers liable for all downloads
Parliament added section 115A to the Copyright Act 1968 to allow site-blocking orders
questions.explanation: After the decision, Parliament created a different remedy: section 115A lets copyright owners apply to the Federal Court for orders requiring carriage service providers to block overseas sites that infringe copyright. This shows parliament responding to a gap revealed by a court decision.

questions.stem: R v Bayliss and Cullen (1986) is a Queensland District Court case in which two doctors charged with unlawfully procuring an abortion were acquitted. What is its significance for law reform?
options: It struck down the Criminal Code as inconsistent with a Commonwealth law on health
It was the first case in which the High Court recognised an implied right to privacy
It set a binding precedent for all Australian states and territories on abortion law
It showed courts applying the Criminal Code before parliament reformed the law
questions.explanation: The judge directed the jury on when an abortion could be lawful under the Criminal Code, and the doctors were acquitted. The law remained in the Code until the Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 (Qld). A District Court decision is not binding on other states.

questions.stem: In Al Masri v Minister for Immigration (2002), the Federal Court held a man's immigration detention unlawful because there was no real likelihood of his removal from Australia in the reasonably foreseeable future. Which concept does the case best show?
options: A tribunal reviewing a visa decision on its merits rather than its legality
The High Court using the external affairs power to implement a treaty
Courts applying the rule of law to limit executive detention under a statute
Parliament overriding a court decision by passing a retrospective law
questions.explanation: The Court interpreted the Migration Act as not authorising indefinite detention where removal was not reasonably practicable, holding the executive to the limits of its legal power. The High Court later took a different view in Al-Kateb v Godwin (2004).

questions.stem: In the 'Kevin and Jennifer' case (2003), the Full Court of the Family Court held that the marriage of Kevin, a transgender man, was valid. Why is the case seen as a landmark?
options: It transferred the power over marriage from the states to the Commonwealth
It recognised a transgender man as a man for the purpose of marriage law
It allowed same-sex couples to marry for the first time in Australia
It declared the Marriage Act 1961 invalid as inconsistent with the Constitution
questions.explanation: The Family Court held that 'man' in marriage law should be given its ordinary contemporary meaning, so Kevin was a man and the marriage was valid. Same-sex marriage became lawful only after parliament amended the Marriage Act in 2017.

questions.stem: A Queensland District Court judge must apply a Court of Appeal decision on the meaning of a section of the Criminal Code, though she thinks it is wrong. Which statement best explains her position?
options: She is bound by the precedent, though parliament could amend the section or a higher court overrule it
She may ignore it, because statutory interpretation never creates binding precedents
She may overrule it, because the District Court hears more criminal trials than the Court of Appeal
She must refer the question to the Governor for a ruling on what parliament intended
questions.explanation: The Court of Appeal is above the District Court in the same hierarchy, so its interpretation of a statute is binding. The precedent can be changed by the Court of Appeal or High Court in a later case, or by parliament amending the Act.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of the High Court of Australia?
options: It reviews government decisions on their merits when a tribunal refuses to
It is the final court of appeal and decides disputes about the Constitution
It hears only criminal trials for serious offences that carry life imprisonment
It advises parliament on whether a bill should be passed before it is debated
questions.explanation: The High Court is the final court of appeal in Australia and interprets the Constitution, including deciding whether laws are within power. It does not give advisory opinions on bills or conduct merits review.

questions.stem: The Fitzgerald Inquiry (1987-1989) investigated:
options: the abolition of the Legislative Council and its effect on democracy
the treatment of children in youth detention centres in Queensland
possible illegal activities and associated police misconduct in Queensland
the causes of the 1974 Brisbane floods and the government's response
questions.explanation: The Commission of Inquiry into Possible Illegal Activities and Associated Police Misconduct, led by Tony Fitzgerald QC, exposed corruption reaching senior police and government. It began in 1987 after media reports, including the ABC's Four Corners program The Moonlight State.

questions.stem: Which outcome of the Fitzgerald Inquiry best shows improved accountability of government in Queensland?
options: Independent bodies were set up to investigate official misconduct
The Legislative Council was restored to act as a house of review over the Assembly
Police were given power to make arrests without warrants for the first time
The Premier became directly elected by voters instead of chosen by parliament
questions.explanation: The inquiry led to the Criminal Justice Commission, a forerunner of the Crime and Corruption Commission, and to the Electoral and Administrative Review Commission, which reviewed electoral and parliamentary processes. The Legislative Council was not restored.

questions.stem: The Fitzgerald Inquiry followed investigative reporting, and its findings led to criminal convictions of a former police commissioner and several ministers. Which conclusion about the rule of law does this best support?
options: Courts cannot convict public officials for conduct carried out while in office
The rule of law applies to police but not to elected members of parliament
No one is above the law, and independent inquiries and media help enforce this
Parliament alone is responsible for holding the executive government to account
questions.explanation: The prosecutions after the inquiry showed that senior officials were subject to the same laws as everyone else. The media's role in exposing misconduct and the inquiry's independent investigation both supported accountability beyond parliament itself.
